title: Alka-Seltzer for Hangover: Does It Work, and Is It Safe?
excerpt: Alka-Seltzer, including the caffeinated Hangover Relief version, is aspirin plus extras. What it can and can't do for a hangover, the stomach risk, and safer timing.
metaDescription: Does Alka-Seltzer help a hangover? What aspirin plus antacid does after drinking, stomach bleeding and sodium risks, safe timing, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Alka-Seltzer can take the edge off a hangover headache and settle an acid stomach, because the original formula is two drugs in one fizzy glass: **aspirin** (a painkiller) and **sodium bicarbonate** (an antacid, basically baking soda). That combination is also why it deserves more caution than its friendly reputation suggests. Aspirin and alcohol both irritate the stomach lining, aspirin thins the blood, and alcohol makes both of those effects worse. Each tablet also carries a surprising amount of sodium. For a healthy adult who had a few drinks, one standard dose the next morning, taken with water once the alcohol has cleared, is usually reasonable. For anyone with stomach problems, a bleeding risk, high blood pressure, or a heavy drinking habit, it's the wrong pick.

**The quick rules:** Don't take Alka-Seltzer *before* or *while* drinking to "prevent" a hangover. Wait until the morning, dissolve the labeled dose in water, and take no more than the label allows in 24 hours. Check which Alka-Seltzer you're holding, because some versions contain aspirin, some don't, and some cold-and-flu versions contain acetaminophen or drowsy antihistamines. If you have 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using aspirin products at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using Alka-Seltzer if** you have had a stomach ulcer or stomach bleeding, take a blood thinner, daily aspirin, other NSAIDs, steroids, or an SSRI antidepressant, have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, are on a low-sodium diet, have asthma, or are pregnant. **Get medical care right away if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, feel faint, or have severe stomach pain after drinking or after taking aspirin. In an emergency, call 911.

## What's Actually in Alka-Seltzer?

"Alka-Seltzer" is a brand family, not a single product. The one most people picture, the foil-wrapped fizzing tablet, is **Alka-Seltzer Original**. Its active ingredients, per the US label, are:

- **Aspirin** (325 mg per tablet), a pain reliever and fever reducer in the NSAID family, the same group as ibuprofen and naproxen.
- **Sodium bicarbonate** (heat-treated, roughly 1,900 mg per tablet), an antacid that neutralizes stomach acid.
- **Citric acid** (1,000 mg per tablet), which reacts with the bicarbonate in water to make the fizz.

When you drop the tablets in water, the citric acid and bicarbonate react and release carbon dioxide bubbles. The aspirin dissolves into a buffered solution rather than sitting in your stomach as a solid pill. The bicarbonate that's left over neutralizes some stomach acid. The usual adult dose is two tablets dissolved in about 4 ounces of water.

**Alka-Seltzer Extra Strength** uses the same idea with more aspirin per tablet (500 mg). Other products under the brand work very differently, and that matters for hangovers:

| Product type | Contains aspirin? | Other key ingredients | Notes for the morning after |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original and Extra Strength fizzing tablets | Yes | Sodium bicarbonate, citric acid | Pain relief plus antacid; stomach-bleeding warning applies |
| Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief (formerly Wake-Up Call) | Yes, 500 mg per tablet | Caffeine, 65 mg per tablet | Targets headache and grogginess; covered in its own section below |
| Heartburn relief versions | Many are aspirin-free | Sodium bicarbonate and citric acid, or calcium carbonate chews | Antacid only, no painkiller |
| Alka-Seltzer Plus (cold and flu) | Varies by version | May contain acetaminophen, antihistamines, decongestants, cough suppressants | Not designed for hangovers; drowsy versions add to alcohol's sedation |

Formulas change and vary by country, so the label in your hand is the only reliable source. Look at the "Drug Facts" box, specifically the "Active ingredients" line and the "Warnings" section.

## Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief: The Caffeine Version

If you bought the box that literally says "Hangover Relief," you're holding a different formula from the original. Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief, sold in the US and previously called **Alka-Seltzer Wake-Up Call**, is a fizzy tablet with two active ingredients:

- **Aspirin, 500 mg per tablet**, more than the 325 mg in Original.
- **Caffeine, 65 mg per tablet**, roughly a small cup of brewed coffee.

The adult dose on the US box is two tablets in water, which works out to about **1,000 mg of aspirin and 130 mg of caffeine**. Check your own package for how often you can repeat it and the 24-hour maximum.

**Why the caffeine is there.** It blocks adenosine, a brain chemical that builds up and makes you feel tired, so it helps with the foggy, slow feeling after a short night. It also makes painkillers work a little better: a Cochrane review of caffeine as a painkiller "helper" found a small but real increase in the number of people who got good pain relief when caffeine was added. At 130 mg it's a moderate amount, but it can make you jittery if you're already shaky, make a racing heart worse, and make it harder to nap later.

**What it does and doesn't do.** It's a reasonable headache-and-grogginess product for a hangover morning, and the dissolved drink can be easier to get down than pills. It does nothing for nausea, dehydration, or poor sleep, and there's no good evidence that it prevents or cures a hangover. In user reviews, the common praise is that it knocks out the headache and wakes people up; the common complaints are that it doesn't help nausea and can upset an already sore stomach. That matches the ingredients.

**What changes compared with Original.** Everything in this article about aspirin and alcohol applies, with a bit more aspirin per dose. Hangover Relief is generally made without Original's large load of sodium bicarbonate, so it doesn't work as an antacid; check the "Other information" section of the box for its sodium content. Three extra rules:

1. **Never take it together with Original Alka-Seltzer** or any other aspirin product. Both contain aspirin, and doubling up is an easy way to go past a safe dose.
2. **Count your caffeine.** Coffee, energy drinks, or caffeinated soda on top of a 130 mg dose add up fast.
3. **Don't take it at bedtime.** Alcohol is still in your stomach, and the caffeine works against the sleep you need.

Skip it, or ask a pharmacist first, if you're sensitive to caffeine, have anxiety or heart rhythm problems, or fit any of the groups listed further down.

## Why Alka-Seltzer and Alcohol Need Care: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Three things are going on when you combine aspirin-based Alka-Seltzer with alcohol.

### 1. Two stomach irritants at once

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly and increases acid production. That's a big part of why your stomach feels raw or burns after a night out (our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains this in detail).

Aspirin adds a second, different kind of stress. Your stomach protects itself with chemical messengers called prostaglandins, which keep the protective mucus layer thick and the blood flow healthy. Aspirin works by blocking the enzymes (called COX enzymes) that make prostaglandins. That's how it reduces pain and inflammation, but it also weakens the stomach's own defenses.

This is the part that surprises people: **the antacid in Alka-Seltzer doesn't cancel out this risk.** Buffering helps the aspirin dissolve and may reduce some direct irritation where the pill touches the stomach wall. But much of aspirin's effect on the stomach comes from blocking prostaglandins throughout the body after it's absorbed, and an antacid can't stop that. Studies comparing buffered and plain aspirin have generally not found that buffering removes the risk of stomach bleeding. That's why the stomach-bleeding warning appears on Alka-Seltzer's label just like it does on a bottle of plain aspirin.

### 2. Thinner blood

Aspirin stops platelets, the small cells that help blood clot, from sticking together. Unlike ibuprofen, aspirin's effect on a platelet is permanent for the life of that platelet, which is about a week to ten days. A single dose has a measurable effect for days.

Alcohol, especially in larger amounts, also affects clotting and irritates blood vessels in the stomach. Put a weakened stomach lining together with slower clotting and you get the reason for the label warning: a small erosion that would normally stop on its own is more likely to bleed.

### 3. Aspirin may raise blood alcohol slightly

Some alcohol is broken down in the stomach before it ever reaches your bloodstream, by an enzyme called gastric alcohol dehydrogenase. A small study published in *JAMA* in 1990 found that taking aspirin before drinking led to higher blood alcohol levels than drinking alone, likely because aspirin interferes with that stomach enzyme. Later studies have been mixed on how big the effect is, but it's one more reason not to take aspirin *before* you drink.

### What the label says

The US Drug Facts label for aspirin products, including Alka-Seltzer Original, carries a stomach-bleeding warning. It says the chance of stomach bleeding is higher if you are age 60 or older, have had stomach ulcers or bleeding problems, take a blood thinner or steroid, take other NSAIDs, **have 3 or more alcoholic drinks every day while using the product**, or take more or for longer than directed. That "3 or more drinks every day" line is the clearest official threshold you'll find. It's about regular drinking, not a single weekend, but it tells you which direction the risk runs.

## Does Alka-Seltzer Actually Help a Hangover?

It can help with two specific symptoms. It does nothing for the cause.

**The headache.** Hangover headaches seem to involve inflammation, and there's long-standing interest in prostaglandins as part of the picture. An NSAID like aspirin is a reasonable tool for that kind of pain. A small Finnish study from 1983 found that tolfenamic acid, another NSAID, taken with drinking, reduced some hangover symptoms. That's a hint, not proof, and nobody has run good modern trials on aspirin or Alka-Seltzer specifically for hangovers.

**The acid stomach.** The bicarbonate neutralizes stomach acid quickly, which can ease heartburn or a sour, burning stomach. If acid is your main problem, though, you don't need aspirin to fix it. An aspirin-free antacid does that job without adding stomach-bleeding risk. Our guides to [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol) and [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) cover those options.

**What it doesn't do.** Alka-Seltzer doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, doesn't clear acetaldehyde (the toxic by-product of alcohol that drives a lot of hangover misery), doesn't fix dehydration in any meaningful way, and doesn't help with poor sleep. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* looked at the trials for hangover remedies and found no compelling evidence that any of them reliably prevents or treats hangovers. That remains broadly true today.

**Why it has a reputation anyway.** Some of Alka-Seltzer's appeal is real (pain relief plus antacid in one dose) and some of it is ritual. You're drinking a glass of water, which helps a little. Fizzy drinks can feel settling. And most hangovers get better over the course of the morning on their own, so whatever you took at 9 a.m. tends to get the credit by noon.

## Is It Safe to Take Alka-Seltzer the Morning After?

For a healthy adult who had a moderate night, doesn't drink heavily day to day, and has none of the risk factors below, a single labeled dose the morning after is generally considered low risk. The aim is to keep the risk low:

1. **Wait until the alcohol has cleared.** Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people. If you were drinking until 2 a.m., you may still have alcohol in your system at 8 a.m.
2. **Eat something first if you can.** Even toast or crackers. Food gives your stomach some cover.
3. **Dissolve it fully in water** and drink the whole glass. Then drink another glass of plain water.
4. **Take one labeled dose,** not a double dose because you feel terrible.
5. **Don't stack painkillers.** Don't combine Alka-Seltzer with ibuprofen, naproxen, or plain aspirin. If you need more pain relief later, talk to a pharmacist rather than layering NSAIDs.
6. **Stop if your stomach gets worse.** Burning that increases, cramping, or any sign of blood means stop and get checked.

### How many tablets and how often?

Follow the label on your specific box, because the limits differ between products. As a general picture of US labeling for Alka-Seltzer Original, adults take 2 tablets dissolved in water every 4 hours as needed, with a lower 24-hour maximum for people 60 and older than for younger adults. Extra Strength has more aspirin per tablet, so its limits are lower and the doses are spaced further apart. Don't use it for pain for more than 10 days without talking to a doctor, which is the standard instruction on aspirin products. For a hangover, you shouldn't need more than one dose. If you do, that's a sign something other than a normal hangover may be going on.

## Taking Alka-Seltzer Before Drinking: A Bad Idea

Some people take Alka-Seltzer before going out or before bed while still drunk, hoping to head off the hangover. This is the worst timing for three reasons:

- **Aspirin may raise your blood alcohol** by interfering with the stomach enzyme that breaks down some alcohol before it's absorbed, as described above.
- **Your stomach is at its most vulnerable** while alcohol is actively irritating it. Adding aspirin at the same moment stacks the two effects together.
- **There is no good evidence** that taking it in advance reduces the hangover. Any benefit for the headache happens when the aspirin is in your system, so taking it the night before mostly wears off by morning.

The same applies to the 3 a.m. "take something before I pass out" dose. You're still drinking, in effect, because the alcohol is still in your blood. Drink water, go to sleep, and deal with the headache in the morning.

## The Sodium Problem Nobody Mentions

The bicarbonate in Alka-Seltzer is *sodium* bicarbonate, and there's a lot of it. Each Alka-Seltzer Original tablet contains roughly 550 to 600 mg of sodium, according to the label. A standard two-tablet dose is well over 1,000 mg, which is close to half of the 2,300 mg daily limit US dietary guidelines recommend for most adults.

For most healthy people, one dose is not a problem. But it matters if you:

- have **high blood pressure** or are on blood pressure medicine
- have **heart failure** or have been told to limit salt
- have **kidney disease**
- are on any **sodium-restricted diet**

The label tells people on a sodium-restricted diet to ask a doctor before using it. If that's you, an aspirin-free and low-sodium antacid, or simply time, water, and food, is a better plan. A big load of sodium bicarbonate can also cause gas, bloating, and, rarely, a disturbance in the body's acid-base balance if it's overused, which is another reason to stick to the label dose.

## Alka-Seltzer vs. Tylenol vs. Advil for a Hangover

Every over-the-counter painkiller has a trade-off after drinking. None of them is risk-free.

| | Alka-Seltzer Original (aspirin + antacid) | Tylenol (acetaminophen) | Advil (ibuprofen) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main concern with alcohol | Stomach bleeding, slower clotting | Liver strain, especially with heavy regular drinking or high doses | Stomach bleeding, kidney strain when dehydrated |
| Helps acid stomach? | Yes, the bicarbonate neutralizes acid | No | No, can make it worse |
| Effect on blood clotting | Strong and lasts days | Minimal | Mild and short-lived |
| Extra concern | High sodium; Reye's syndrome risk in children and teens | Hidden acetaminophen in combination products | Take with food |

In short:

- **Tylenol** is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver. The danger is concentrated in high doses, doubling up on products, and regular heavy drinking. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver chemistry.
- **Ibuprofen and aspirin** are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach. Aspirin's effect on clotting lasts longer than ibuprofen's. See our [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) guides.
- **Alka-Seltzer Original** is aspirin with a built-in antacid. The antacid makes it more pleasant on a sour stomach, but it doesn't make the aspirin safer for your stomach lining.

If you want a side-by-side decision guide, our article on [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) walks through which one to reach for depending on how you feel and how much you drank.

## What About Alka-Seltzer Plus and Alcohol?

Alka-Seltzer Plus is the cold-and-flu line, and it's a different product from the hangover-friendly image of the original. Depending on the version, it may contain:

- **Acetaminophen,** which brings the liver concerns covered in our Tylenol guide, and which is easy to double up on without realizing it.
- **Aspirin,** in some versions, which brings the stomach-bleeding concerns covered above.
- **Antihistamines** such as chlorpheniramine or doxylamine, which cause drowsiness. Alcohol makes that drowsiness much stronger, slows your reactions, and can make breathing shallower in people who've had a lot to drink.
- **Decongestants** such as phenylephrine, which can raise heart rate and blood pressure.
- **Cough suppressants** such as dextromethorphan, which can add dizziness and sedation alongside alcohol.

Most of these products carry warnings to avoid alcohol or to ask a doctor if you drink. They're not designed for hangovers, and using a "nighttime" or drowsy version while alcohol is still in your system is a genuinely bad combination. If you're sick and have been drinking, wait until the alcohol has cleared and read the full label, or ask a pharmacist which single-ingredient product fits your symptoms.

## Who Should Skip Alka-Seltzer After Drinking

Don't use aspirin-containing Alka-Seltzer for a hangover, and talk to a doctor or pharmacist instead, if you:

- **Have had a stomach ulcer, stomach bleeding, or gastritis**, or currently have heartburn that keeps coming back.
- **Take a blood thinner** such as warfarin, apixaban, or rivaroxaban, or an antiplatelet drug such as clopidogrel.
- **Already take daily low-dose aspirin** for your heart. Adding more aspirin isn't the answer, and some NSAIDs can interfere with low-dose aspirin's heart protection.
- **Take other NSAIDs, steroids such as prednisone, or SSRI antidepressants**, all of which raise bleeding risk alongside aspirin.
- **Are 60 or older**, which the label lists as a risk factor for stomach bleeding.
- **Drink 3 or more drinks most days.**
- **Have high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease, or a salt-restricted diet**, because of the sodium.
- **Have asthma that gets worse with aspirin**, or are allergic to aspirin or other NSAIDs.
- **Are pregnant**, especially later in pregnancy, unless a doctor has told you to take aspirin.
- **Are under 19.** Aspirin products carry a warning about Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness, in children and teenagers, especially while recovering from flu or chickenpox. (Teenagers shouldn't be drinking either, but if a teen is unwell after drinking, don't reach for aspirin.)
- **Have gout or take diabetes medicines**, which the label lists as reasons to ask a doctor first.

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless, and they fade within a day. Some symptoms are not a normal hangover, and they need care, not another fizzy glass.

> **Get medical help right away if you or someone else:**
> - vomits blood, or vomit that looks like dark coffee grounds
> - has black, sticky, or tarry stools, or stools with blood in them
> - has severe stomach pain that doesn't ease, or pain that spreads to the back
> - feels faint, dizzy when standing, or looks very pale after drinking or taking aspirin
> - can't keep any fluids down for many hours
> - is confused, very hard to wake, has slow or irregular breathing, or has a seizure (these are signs of alcohol poisoning; call 911)
> - has ringing in the ears, rapid breathing, or confusion after taking more aspirin than the label allows (possible aspirin overdose; call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US, or 911)

**See a doctor soon (not an emergency) if** you regularly need a painkiller or antacid after drinking, you get heartburn or stomach pain that lasts beyond the hangover, or you notice that your hangovers are getting worse. Recurring stomach symptoms after drinking can be a sign of gastritis or an ulcer, which are very treatable but need a proper diagnosis.

If you drink most days and feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you *stop*, that's not a hangover. It can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous to manage alone. Talk to a doctor before cutting back suddenly; they can help you do it safely.

## A Better Plan for the Morning After

Alka-Seltzer treats two symptoms. If you're reaching for it often, the more useful fixes are upstream:

- **Pace yourself.** Fewer drinks, spaced out, with water between them, is still the most reliable way to have a better morning. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food in the stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed and gives your stomach lining some protection.
- **Handle the stomach and the headache separately.** If your main problem is acid or nausea, an aspirin-free antacid, bland food, and small sips of fluid are a gentler start. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ideas. If the headache is the main problem, choose one painkiller based on your own risk factors and take it with food.
- **Rehydrate properly.** Plain water is fine for most people. If you've been sick or sweating, an electrolyte drink can help more than a glass of salty fizz.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality, and a lot of next-day misery is simple sleep debt.

Some people also try supplements. Here's an honest view of the one this site focuses on:

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. Some people take it with drinking and feel their mornings are better, but there is no good evidence that it reliably prevents hangovers, and it is not a painkiller or an antacid. It also doesn't change any of the aspirin or alcohol warnings above. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and ask your pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Alka-Seltzer Original is **aspirin plus an antacid**. It can help a hangover headache and an acid stomach, but it doesn't treat the hangover itself.
- The antacid **does not make the aspirin safe for your stomach**. Aspirin and alcohol together raise the risk of stomach bleeding, and aspirin thins the blood for days.
- **Take it the morning after, not before or during drinking**, once the alcohol has cleared, with food and water, at the labeled dose only.
- **Watch the sodium** if you have high blood pressure, heart or kidney problems, or a salt-restricted diet.
- **Read the label.** Some Alka-Seltzer products contain no aspirin, and some cold-and-flu versions contain acetaminophen or drowsy antihistamines that don't mix with alcohol.
- If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have stomach problems, or take blood thinners, talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using it.
- Vomiting blood, black stools, severe stomach pain, or fainting need medical care right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Alka-Seltzer good for a hangover?**

It can help two symptoms: the headache (from the aspirin) and an acid or sour stomach (from the sodium bicarbonate). It doesn't speed up how your body clears alcohol or fix the underlying causes of a hangover. For a healthy adult, one labeled dose the morning after is generally reasonable, but it isn't the best choice for anyone with stomach problems, a bleeding risk, or high blood pressure.

**Can you take Alka-Seltzer after drinking alcohol?**

Most healthy adults who drank moderately can take one labeled dose the next morning, once the alcohol has cleared, with water and ideally some food. The label's stomach-bleeding warning specifically mentions people who have 3 or more drinks every day. If that describes you, or you have had ulcers, take blood thinners, or are 60 or older, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Should I take Alka-Seltzer before drinking to prevent a hangover?**

No. There is no good evidence that taking it in advance reduces a hangover. Aspirin taken before drinking may raise your blood alcohol level slightly, and it adds stress to your stomach lining at the same time alcohol is irritating it. If you need it, take it the morning after.

**How long after drinking can I take Alka-Seltzer?**

There's no single official waiting time. A sensible approach is to wait until the alcohol is out of your system (the body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies widely), eat something, and then take one labeled dose. After a very heavy night, that may mean waiting until late morning.

**Does the antacid in Alka-Seltzer protect your stomach from the aspirin?**

Not in the way most people assume. Buffering helps the aspirin dissolve and may reduce some direct irritation, but a large part of aspirin's effect on the stomach comes from blocking protective prostaglandins after it's absorbed. That's why Alka-Seltzer Original carries the same stomach-bleeding warning as plain aspirin.

**Is there an Alka-Seltzer without aspirin?**

Yes. Several Alka-Seltzer heartburn products are aspirin-free and work only as antacids. They can help with acid or heartburn after drinking but won't help the headache. Check the "Active ingredients" line on the Drug Facts label, because formulas vary between products and countries.

**Is Alka-Seltzer Plus safe with alcohol?**

Generally it's best avoided while alcohol is still in your system. Depending on the version, Alka-Seltzer Plus can contain acetaminophen, aspirin, drowsy antihistamines, decongestants, or cough suppressants. The antihistamines and cough suppressants add to alcohol's sedation, and acetaminophen adds liver strain. Read the full label and wait until the alcohol has cleared, or ask a pharmacist.

**Is Alka-Seltzer better than Tylenol or Advil for a hangover?**

None is clearly better; they have different risks. Tylenol is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver, especially with high doses or regular heavy drinking. Advil and Alka-Seltzer are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach, and aspirin's blood-thinning effect lasts longer than ibuprofen's. Alka-Seltzer's added antacid helps an acid stomach but also adds a lot of sodium. Pick one based on your own health, take it with food, and don't combine them.

**How much sodium is in Alka-Seltzer?**

A lot for a medicine. Each Alka-Seltzer Original tablet contains roughly 550 to 600 mg of sodium according to the label, so a two-tablet dose is over 1,000 mg, close to half of the 2,300 mg daily limit recommended for most adults. People with high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease, or a salt-restricted diet should ask a doctor before using it.

**Is Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief the same as original Alka-Seltzer?**

No. Original Alka-Seltzer has 325 mg of aspirin per tablet plus a large amount of sodium bicarbonate and citric acid, which act as an antacid. Hangover Relief, previously sold as Alka-Seltzer Wake-Up Call, has 500 mg of aspirin and 65 mg of caffeine per tablet. Both contain aspirin, so never take them together.

**Can I take Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief with coffee?**

You can, but count the caffeine. A two-tablet dose has about 130 mg of caffeine, and a large coffee can add a lot more. Too much caffeine on a hangover morning can make shakiness, a racing heart, and anxiety worse. If you're sensitive to caffeine, skip the coffee or choose a caffeine-free option.

The antihistamines and cough suppressants add to alcohol's sedation, and acetaminophen adds liver strain. Read the full label and wait until the alcohol has cleared, or ask a pharmacist.

faq.question: Is Alka-Seltzer better than Tylenol or Advil for a hangover?
faq.answer: None is clearly better; they have different risks. Tylenol is easier on the stomach but harder on the liver, especially with high doses or regular heavy drinking. Advil and Alka-Seltzer are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach, and aspirin's blood-thinning effect lasts longer than ibuprofen's. Alka-Seltzer's added antacid helps an acid stomach but also adds a lot of sodium. Pick one based on your own health, take it with food, and don't combine them.

faq.question: How much sodium is in Alka-Seltzer?
faq.answer: A lot for a medicine. Each Alka-Seltzer Original tablet contains roughly 550 to 600 mg of sodium according to the label, so a two-tablet dose is over 1,000 mg, close to half of the 2,300 mg daily limit recommended for most adults. People with high blood pressure, heart failure, kidney disease, or a salt-restricted diet should ask a doctor before using it.

faq.question: Is Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief the same as original Alka-Seltzer?
faq.answer: No. Original Alka-Seltzer has 325 mg of aspirin per tablet plus a large amount of sodium bicarbonate and citric acid, which act as an antacid. Hangover Relief, previously sold as Alka-Seltzer Wake-Up Call, has 500 mg of aspirin and 65 mg of caffeine per tablet. Both contain aspirin, so never take them together.

faq.question: Can I take Alka-Seltzer Hangover Relief with coffee?
faq.answer: You can, but count the caffeine. A two-tablet dose has about 130 mg of caffeine, and a large coffee can add a lot more. Too much caffeine on a hangover morning can make shakiness, a racing heart, and anxiety worse. If you're sensitive to caffeine, skip the coffee or choose a caffeine-free option.
